background.definition: Croup is a respiratory illness characterized by abrupt onset of barky cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, and respiratory distress.

list.listitem: Peak incidence is between 1 and 2 years of age: 60 per 1000 persons/y.
Peak incidence is during fall and winter months.
Most common: parainfluenza virus (types 1, 2, and 3), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), human rhinovirus.
Less common: influenza virus, coronavirus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, adenovirus, enterovirus, and herpes simplex.
Gastroesophageal reflux has been associated with recurrent croup.
Croup is thought to be caused by edema of the larynx and trachea that has been triggered by a recent viral infection. This leads to irritation of the subglottic region.
As the narrowing at the subglottic region progresses, children compensate by breathing more quickly and deeply.
Stridor is heard as turbulent air passes through the subglottic narrowing.
Diagnosis is based on history and physical examination findings: seal-like barky cough, inspiratory stridor, and hoarseness. C
The clinical severity of croup helps direct treatment options. C
Imaging and diagnostic testing are not routinely recommended. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Wheezing rather than stridor; also edema and rash
High fever, toxic appearance, poor response to croup treatment
Possible history of choking event, no viral symptoms
No viral symptoms, airway obstruction only
Sudden onset of symptoms with high fever, drooling, dysphagia and sitting in "sniffing position"
Rarely presents with stridor, usually throat pain and fever
Transient, recurrent episodes of stridor without fever, possible allergy mediated

list.listitem: The diagnosis is based on history and physical examination. Typical symptoms include stridor, seal-like barky cough, and hoarseness.
Symptoms are most common in the late evening and night and are abrupt in onset. They are often preceded by nonspecific cough, fever, and rhinorrhea.
Physical examination often reveals fever, chest wall retractions, stridor, moderate tachypnea, and tachycardia.
Four levels of croup severity are determined by clinical presentation and examination (see ).

In a case series of 203 children with acute upper airway obstruction presenting to an Australian pediatric intensive care unit, the presence of drooling had a moderate sensitivity (0.79, 95% CI 0.70-0.86) and high specificity (0.94, 95% CI 0.88-0.97) for epiglottitis while coughing had a high sensitivity (1.00, 95% CI 0.96-1.00) and high specificity (0.98, 95% CI 0.93-0.99) for croup.
Laboratory and radiologic tests are not needed to make the diagnosis. Avoid laboratory tests while the patient is in respiratory distress.

Although not recommended for routine use, lateral anteroposterior neck views may show the "steeple sign," cone-shaped narrowing of subglottic area. Avoid radiologic assessments while the patient is in respiratory distress. Viral cultures or rapid viral antigen tests do not help with the routine management.

However, a study using a pediatric health information system database found marked hospital to hospital variability in the use of tests and interventions for croup that are not routinely recommended (up to a 5-fold difference).

Most children with recurrent croup have no abnormal findings on bronchoscopy. Between 5% and 10% have moderate to severe (grade II to grade IV) subglottic stenosis, based on case-series data.
A systematic review of 5 studies with 455 patients found that the most common bronchoscopic findings were subglottic stenosis, reflux changes, and broncho- or tracheomalacia. However, only 9% of children with recurrent croup had clinically significant findings. Risk factors for moderate to severe abnormal finding include a history of previous intubation (RR = 9.8), prematurity (RR = 6.4), or inpatient consultation (RR = 5.3).
The Syracuse Croup score is somewhat more complex than the system proposed in but can also be used to assess the likelihood that a child will require intubation.
It uses the respiratory rate, pulse rate, and presence or absence of sternal retractions, cyanosis, or stridor. It has been prospectively validated.
See algorithm in for an approach to management based on clinical severity upon presentation.
Give oral glucocorticoids to all patients who present with croup symptoms. Recent studies suggest that oral dexamethasone doses of 0.15 mg/kg are as effective as 0.6 mg/kg. A

Give nebulized epinephrine, either racemic or the L-isomer (standard epinephrine), to patients with severe respiratory distress. Dose: racemic epinephrine 0.5 mL of 2.25% solution diluted in 3 mL of normal saline or sterile water delivered via nebulizer OR L-epinephrine 1:1000 solution 5 mL delivered via nebulizer. B

Admission is appropriate for patients with persistent stridor and retractions 4 hours after an oral steroid has been given. If the patient develops recurrent lethargy or agitation, admit to pediatric ICU. C
Make the child as comfortable as possible in the emergency department (ED); do not agitate the child with unnecessary treatment.
Provide blow-by oxygen to those with hypoxia. Humidified air is not recommended for treatment.

Give a single oral dose of dexamethasone (0.6 mg/kg) to all patients who present with croup. A Cochrane review of 43 studies with 4565 children concluded that glucocorticoids bring about clinical improvement in children with croup within 2 hours, an effect that persists for 24 hours. A smaller dose appears to be equally effective (0.15 mg/kg). Use of glucocorticoids (dexamethasone or budesonide) is associated with a lower rate of epinephrine use, fever, return visits, and admissions, as well as a shorter time spent in hospital (NNT = 5). In one RCT, no differences were found for those treated with dexamethasone (0.6 mg/kg) or prednisolone (2 mg/kg/d for 3 days) on symptom duration or use of healthcare. The difference between glucocorticoids and placebo is no longer significant at 24 hours.

Authors of a Cochrane review of systematic reviews confirmed a benefit of systemic corticosteroids for children with asthma or croup with respect to fewer admissions, shorter (over 8 hours) hospital stay, and fewer relapses requiring admission without differences in GI bleeding, abdominal pain, behavioral effects or hypertension compared to placebo..
Nebulized budesonide is also effective in treating croup. This is generally reserved for severe croup in patients who are vomiting or too distressed to take oral medications.

Use nebulized epinephrine, either racemic or the L-isomer (standard epinephrine), in patients with severe respiratory distress. Improvement occurs within minutes and begins to wear off after 1 or 2 hours. In a Cochrane review, one trial of L-epinephrine showed significant reduction in croup score compared with racemic epinephrine at 2 hours. Dose: racemic epinephrine 0.25-0.5 mL/dose of 2.25% solution diluted in 3 mL of normal saline or sterile water delivered via nebulizer OR L-epinephrine 5 mL/dose of 1:1000 solution delivered via nebulizer.
The nebulized epinephrine dose can be repeated for children with near respiratory failure; however, it should not be given continuously.

Heliox (helium-oxygen mixture) inhalation appears to be no more effective than 30% oxygen in children with mild croup but may be useful for moderate to severe croup; two of three small trials found some early benefit of heliox over oxygen alone, although differences did not persist after 2 to 4 hours.

Consider hospitalization to regular floor if the patient has continued moderate respiratory distress including stridor at rest and chest wall retractions at least 4 hours after receiving dexamethasone. Also consider hospitalization if the patient requires ≥2 nebulized epinephrine treatments.
If the patient has respiratory distress with recurrent severe episodes of agitation or lethargy, admit to pediatric ICU.
Consider admission if the family has inadequate transportation or significant anxiety or if there have been recurrent ED visits within 24 hours.
Intubation may be required in a small number of hospitalized patients (<1%).

In a case series of 77 intubated children with croup, the median duration of intubation was 60 hours and primary extubation failure occurred in 6.5% of patients. Non-urgent tracheostomy was performed in one child and there was one death from hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy.
Monitor respiratory status, including vital signs and focused clinical examination frequently.
Most children with croup do not require specific follow-up. Consider follow-up with primary care provider for patients who have had stridor for more than 1 week. C
Most mild croup symptoms resolve within 48 hours, but small proportions of children have symptoms that persist for up to 1 week. B
The use of glucocorticoids in patients with croup results in a lower rate of epinephrine use, fever, return visits, and admissions, as well as shorter time spent in hospital. A
If a child develops mild respiratory distress, cool night air may provide relief.
Use of humidified air or a steamy bathroom has not proved to be effective.
If the child develops more significant distress but is not agitated or cyanotic, the parents can safely drive their child to the nearest ED.
If the child develops severe agitation and/or cyanosis, the parents should call 911.

algorithm.title: Croup: Management (Based on Severity at Presentation).

cell.label: Assess severity ().
cell.path: Mild (no stridor or retractions at rest)
Moderate (stridor and retractions at rest, no agitation)
Severe (stridor and retractions with agitation or lethargy)

cell.label: Minimize intervention. Give oral dexamethasone (0.6 mg/kg). Retractions and stridor improve?
No or minimal improvement by 4 h: consider hospitalization.
Minimize intervention. Provide blow-by oxygen if patient is cyanotic. Give oral dexamethasone (0.6 mg/kg); may repeat once. Give nebulized epinephrine. Good response?
Observe for 2 h. Recurrence of severe respiratory distress?

Consider hospitalization if: (1) patient received steroid >4 hours ago, (2) continued moderate respiratory distress (stridor and retractions at rest) without agitation or lethargy, or (3) cannot ensure adequate observation and follow-up at home.
Repeat nebulized epinephrine, contact ICU for admission.

feature.caption: Four Levels of Croup Severity.
feature.feature_body:
Mild Occasional Barky Cough, No Stridor at Rest, Mild Retractions
Moderate Frequent barky cough, stridor at rest, retractions at rest, minimal agitation
Severe Frequent barky cough, prominent stridor, significant retractions, marked distress and agitation
Impending respiratory failure Barky cough, stridor at rest, retractions, lethargy or decreased level of consciousness, often dusky without supplemental oxygenation
